name: Classical Computers Keep Up
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Moving Goalposts of Quantum Advantage
lesson.summary: Nearly every publicized quantum computing milestone has been followed within months or years by a classical algorithm or classical hardware advance that closes much of the claimed gap, a pattern that should temper any single headline about quantum computers beating classical ones.
lesson.body:
A recurring pattern runs through the short history of quantum computing claims. A quantum result is announced with a dramatic classical comparison, and then classical computer scientists, often working from the same published data, find a smarter classical algorithm or a better use of classical hardware that substantially narrows or erases the gap. This has happened often enough that it deserves to be treated as a general lesson rather than a series of unrelated surprises, and it connects directly to why there is no real-world quantum advantage yet: the classical baseline used in most quantum advantage claims turns out to be a moving target rather than a fixed wall.

The clearest case is Google's 2019 Sycamore claim, covered in detail later in this guide, where the original estimate of ten thousand years of classical supercomputer time was challenged within days by IBM researchers arguing that a more careful classical simulation, using far more disk and memory, could do the same job in a few days rather than millennia. Subsequent academic papers using tensor network simulation techniques pushed the estimated or demonstrated classical time down further still, in some analyses to well under a day on large computing clusters, though the exact figures have shifted across several papers and depend heavily on assumptions about available hardware, so they are best read as evolving estimates rather than settled numbers.

The same dynamic shows up with D-Wave's quantum annealers, covered elsewhere in this guide. Every few years, D-Wave or its academic collaborators publish a result showing their hardware outperforming classical methods on some optimization or sampling task, and every few years, other researchers respond with an improved classical simulated annealing approach or another classical heuristic that matches or beats it. Over more than a decade of this back and forth, no D-Wave result has produced a lasting, uncontested demonstration of quantum advantage on a problem anyone outside the debate particularly cares about solving.

Why does this keep happening? Partly because quantum advantage claims are, almost by construction, claims about the current best known classical algorithm, and best known is a moving frontier rather than a law of nature. Classical algorithms research is a mature field with strong incentives, mostly reputational and occasionally financial, to respond quickly to a quantum challenge, while quantum hardware improves comparatively slowly because of noise and engineering constraints. Classical hardware itself, while past the fastest years of historical scaling, continues to improve steadily, and specialized classical accelerators such as GPUs have gotten dramatically better at exactly the kind of large-scale linear algebra and sampling that these comparisons involve.

None of this proves quantum computers will never pull decisively and durably ahead. It does mean that any specific advantage claim should be read as provisional at the moment it is published, and that the more interesting long-run question is not whether a quantum computer beat one particular classical program in one particular month, but whether the gap, adjusted for classical responses over the following years, is trending in a durable direction.
